treams-rs is release-ready on the branch claude/release-readiness: 44 commits on top of main, pushed, no PR opened. The full local gate passes on Python 3.12, and main hadn't moved, so the branch applies cleanly today.

Dependencies

  • Rust: complex-bessel 0.2 → 0.3 plus a full cargo update; everything else was already at its latest release.
  • Python:
    • advect is now allowed up to <0.4 (0.3.0 tested), jax up to <0.12, and NumPy is capped at the tested <2.6.
    • Dev tools are at their latest versions, and uv is now 0.12.22.
    • The upstream treams package the tests compare against moved from 0.4.5 to 0.4.7.
  • GitHub Actions: all pinned to the same commits as advect's.

Test matrix (as in advect)

  • Python 3.12–3.15 and NumPy 2.1–2.5.
  • The lowest and newest supported versions of Advect, JAX, PyTorch and h5py.
  • Rust on 1.94 and current stable, cargo-deny, the wheel license check, a secret scan, Codecov, docs, and a single "CI Success" job that gates releases.

Release process (as in advect)

  • A repository-dispatch trigger builds the full wheel family (5 platforms × 4 Python versions) plus the sdist.
  • It publishes to TestPyPI and checks the install, then waits for your approval and checks the tag.
  • After that it publishes versioned docs, the GitHub Release and PyPI, and checks the public install. RELEASING.md lists the steps, including what's different for 0.1.0.

Public and docs

  • A new mkdocs site using advect's theme (no playground), versioned with mike.
  • The "private" wording is gone, README links are absolute, and SECURITY.md is added.
  • Wheels now ship the license texts of the Rust crates they contain, with a check that fails when they go stale.

Verified locally: everything passes on Python 3.12:

  • just check and the full test suite (2386 passed, 0 skipped);
  • the strict docs build, the license and cargo-deny checks, just check-wheel, and the release-guard self-test;
  • workflow lint and the secret scan over the full history.

The 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15 lanes, the NumPy floor and the framework lower/latest lanes were also run with the exact CI commands and pass.

Not verified: GitHub's API is blocked from here, so these will first run on GitHub:

  • the macOS, Windows and Linux arm64 wheel builds;
  • the Codecov upload;
  • TestPyPI/PyPI publishing;
  • Pages serving the versioned docs.

The headless-Chrome docs check also wasn't re-run after the last fixes.

Gaps

  • Python 3.14/3.15 test coverage is narrower. Upstream treams doesn't install there, so 47 comparison test modules aren't collected and roughly a fifth of the suite runs; the test summary lists them. Moving import treams into the tests that actually use it would bring back about 230 tests, but that touches test files under active edit.
  • No 3.15 wheels upstream for [io] and [torch]. h5py and PyTorch don't publish 3.15 wheels on PyPI yet, so those two extras can't install from wheels on 3.15; the README says so.
  • Library-code follow-ups I didn't make because of the parallel work: treams_rs.__version__ (worth adding before tagging 0.1.0), the python -m treams_rs program name, and a "thorough" Hypothesis lane.

Decisions for you

  • License metadata: it says MIT, but the package contains code adapted from SciPy under BSD-3-Clause. MIT AND BSD-3-Clause is probably the accurate declaration; I left that legal call to you.
  • Codecov patch target: I copied advect's 90% patch target. It may often show red on PRs; making it informational would stop that.
  • advect's other pre-commit hooks (typos, taplo, markdownlint, commitizen): not added, because they'd reformat many files under active edit.

Before the first release, follow the checklist in RELEASING.md: make the repo public, register pending trusted publishers on PyPI and TestPyPI, create the testpypi/pypi/release environments, enable Codecov, Pages and private vulnerability reporting, and add a tag ruleset. As main changes over the next day, the branch will need a rebase. Conflicts will most likely be in uv.lock (re-run uv lock) and docs/api.md (re-run just docs), and after Rust dependency changes run just licenses.

items.html: Everything is green and pushed. Cleaning up the scratch worktrees:

treams-rs can now be released as MIT-only, and every one of advect's pre-commit hooks is in. The branch is pushed (55 commits on top of main, no PR) and the full local check suite passes on it.

Licensing — it's MIT.

  • The only non-MIT code was crates/treams-core/src/legendre.rs (real-degree Legendre functions). It was adapted from SciPy's XSF code, which is BSD-3-Clause and itself based on Zhang & Jin's Fortran under an informal "permission granted to use code in programs" notice. An audit of everything that ships found nothing else derived from non-MIT code.
  • I replaced that file with a clean-room rewrite. One agent wrote a behavioral spec from the old code. A second agent, who never saw the old code or XSF, implemented it from the published math reference (DLMF). A third checked the result: no shared lines or distinctive constants with the old code, results match high-precision references to within 6.4e-15, and it runs 0.33–0.64× the old time.
  • LICENSE.xsf is gone and license = "MIT" stays. Wheels also bundle a few Rust libraries under other permissive licenses (Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause). They can't be removed without large refactors, and they only require shipping their license texts, which the wheels already do. A strict reading of the packaging standard would list those licenses in the wheel metadata. It can't be split between the source and binary packages, though, and declaring only the project's own license is what NumPy and the other Rust-backed packages surveyed do. pyproject.toml, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and the README now say this. A new test checks the license field is valid SPDX, which PyPI enforces and maturin doesn't.

The old Legendre code had two real accuracy bugs, both reachable through special.lpmv:

  • For large orders at arguments between about −0.4 and −0.1, errors reached 52%. For example, lpmv(121, 127.9, -0.34) returned 2.73e242 instead of 2.11e242.
  • For degrees within 1e-3 of an integer near −1, results were off by up to 34 orders of magnitude.

The rewrite fixes both, both cases are now regression tests, and docs/status.md records them. The repo's own accuracy check now passes 530 cases with a worst error of 1.64e-13.

Pre-commit hooks. markdownlint, taplo, typos, commitizen (commit-message check), rustfmt.toml and .cargo/config.toml are all added at their latest versions. They run in CI through just check. Specifics:

  • Not carried over: advect's setting that forces hooks onto Python 3.12, because this repo's dev environments run 3.12–3.15. The reason is in .pre-commit-config.yaml and docs/development.md.
  • markdownlint exposed a live docs bug: the published API page rendered Cluster.__init__ as "Cluster.init". The docs generator is fixed now; this touched python/treams_rs/support.py, which produces that page.
  • typos: I allowlisted only the genuine hits (a Lean variable name, a test variable, verbatim upstream license text), each limited to its file type.
  • When rebasing onto main: the formatting-only commits (style: format TOML with taplo, style: apply markdownlint fixes) should be regenerated with the hooks rather than merged by hand.

One pre-existing flaky test, now fixed. A Rust property test in polar.rs (cartesian_translation_and_all_polar_adjoints) failed on main too, about 1 run in 75 per Rust CI lane. The gradient code is correct; the test's numerical check was too noisy for large values. I switched it to the more robust check its neighbouring test already uses. It passes 20,000 random cases on both Rust toolchains and still fails the way it should with the old check. This is a small edit in a test under the other conversation's active work, so expect it in a rebase.

text: wait does this mean we found a bug in scipy’s legendre?

items.html: The sweep's claim is much stronger than expected, so I'm reading the root-cause analysis and the adversarial verifier's verdict before accepting it:

Yes, SciPy's scipy.special.lpmv has real bugs for real (non-integer) degree. It's just not the same symptom we had.

At our two example points SciPy returns NaN rather than a wrong number. But across the wider range it's often silently wrong. I confirmed the headline cases myself:

Call SciPy 1.16.3 True value (mpmath) treams-rs (new)
lpmv(15, 50.5, -0.99) 9.17e27 **−**1.27e28 (wrong sign) −1.27e28 ✓
lpmv(30, 100.5, -0.99) −1.73e84 −5.27e65 ✓
lpmv(-83, 83.5, -0.9999) 4.72e300 −35.95 ✓
lpmv(50, 60.5, -0.3) 0.7% off −1.434e84 ✓
lpmv(-100, 100.5, 0.0) inf 1.30e-189 ✓
lpmv(121, 127.9, -0.34) nan 2.11e242 ✓

How widespread it is

  • Versions: SciPy 1.16.3, 1.18.1 (latest) and the current main of XSF, SciPy's special-functions library, give bit-identical output on all 131k test points.
  • Below degree ~30: essentially accurate.
  • Above degree ~30: about 10% of uniformly sampled valid inputs come back silently wrong, mostly with no warning even under errstate(all='raise'). Another ~6% return NaN or inf where the true value fits in a double.
  • Docs: the docstring states no degree or accuracy limit.
  • Tests: SciPy's own accuracy test for lpmv only covers degree ≤ 11.3 and order ≤ 5.

Why

  • The degree recursion is numerically unstable: it loses everything even when started from correctly rounded values.
  • A series is cut off at 100 terms with no convergence check.
  • An intermediate gamma-function product overflows even when the final result doesn't.
  • A guard skips the negative-order conversion when |P| ≥ 1e300, so lpmv(-83, …) returns lpmv(83, …).

A line-by-line Python copy of SciPy's algorithm reproduces its output bit for bit, and the true values were cross-checked with an independent integral method.

What it means for treams-rs's old code: both of our old defects were inherited from these same algorithm flaws. In those regions SciPy usually overflows first and returns NaN or inf. Our port's rescaling avoided the overflow, so the same flaws showed up as wrong finite numbers instead. The clean-room rewrite gets all of these cases right.

Upstream: a keyword search of SciPy's issues found no existing report. It wasn't exhaustive, so I can't rule out a duplicate. Related history: a 2010 issue (#1822) about blow-ups above degree ~22, whose fix added the recursion that is now unstable, and a still-open request (#1862) to extend lpmv's domain. SciPy's newer assoc_legendre_p rejects non-integer degree, so lpmv is still its only real-degree routine.

I haven't filed anything. If you want, I can draft a SciPy issue with these reproducers and the root-cause notes for you to post.

text: worth it to file an issue and open apr?

items.html:
Filing the issue: yes. A PR: not yet, and probably not the full rewrite.

The issue is clearly worth filing.

  • SciPy's lpmv silently returns wrong values for ordinary inputs, sometimes with the wrong sign, in the latest release and in current main of XSF (SciPy's special-functions library). Nothing in the docs warns about it.
  • It's cheap to report. We already have minimal reproducers, high-precision true values cross-checked by two independent methods, and a root cause traced to specific mechanisms.
  • I found no existing report, but the keyword search wasn't exhaustive. Do a quick search before posting.
  • I'd file it on scipy/scipy, since users hit it through scipy.special.lpmv, and mention that the code lives in XSF.
  • It should come from your account. I can't post there from this session, which only has access to your two repos.

A PR is worth it only in a different shape than you might expect.

  • A direct port of our rewrite is a poor fit. It's about 1,600 lines of Rust with a custom extended-exponent number type; XSF is C++ templates. That's a large port and a big review burden on code SciPy treats as legacy. Licensing isn't a blocker (you wrote it and can contribute it under BSD-3), but nobody has asked for it yet.
  • Small targeted fixes are reasonable. Two flaws have contained fixes: the negative-order guard (lpmv(-83, …) returning lpmv(83, …)), and the 100-term series cap with no convergence check. Documenting the accurate range would also help. The unstable degree recursion behind most of the silently wrong values is not a small patch, so these fixes would only reduce the problem.
  • Maintainers may prefer another target. They may rather add real-degree support to the newer assoc_legendre_p (there's an open request, #22937) than fix lpmv.

So I'd file the issue first and offer a fix in it: either the targeted patches or the new algorithm, with our MIT implementation and 131k-point test data as a reference. Write the PR only after they say which they want. That costs you about 15 minutes now, versus days of C++ porting and review cycles that would compete with the treams-rs release.

I can draft the issue text now (reproducers, the version matrix, root-cause summary, related history #1822/#1862/#22937, and an offer to contribute) as a file for you to paste. Want that?
